items.title: 10.1 Force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field

source_refs.note: Topic 10.1 with Figs. 10.2 to 10.4, Example 10.1 and the side boxes (PDF 230-232, printed 227-229). The print's description of Fig. 10.2 (force to the left with N above S and current out of the page) is flagged for review.

blocks.text: It has been observed experimentally that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. Consider a straight conductor carrying a steady current, placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, with the current directed out of the paper (Fig. 10.2). Just as two magnets exert forces on each other through their magnetic fields, a current-carrying conductor experiences a force due to the interaction between its own magnetic field and the external magnetic field.

The magnetic field produced by the current and the external uniform field reinforce each other on one side of the conductor and cancel each other on the other side. Consequently the conductor moves towards the side where the field is weaker; in the book's Fig. 10.2 this is the left. Thus the force F is perpendicular to both the conductor and the magnetic field.

blocks.title: Fleming's left-hand rule
blocks.text: Position your left hand such that the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger points in the direction of the current; the thumb will then point in the direction of the force (Fig. 10.3). The direction of the force can also be found with the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand from the current to the magnetic field through the small angle; the stretched thumb indicates the direction of the force.

Experimentally, the magnitude of the force on a conductor placed inside a magnetic field is directly proportional to the current I in the conductor, the length L of the conductor and the strength of the external magnetic field B. The strength of the magnetic field is also known as the magnetic induction B, which has the same direction as the field. Thus the force on a conductor of length L carrying a current I placed perpendicular to a field of strength B is F proportional to BIL, or F = kBIL. In SI units k = 1, therefore F = BIL ... (10.1).

blocks.title: Magnetic induction (field strength) B
blocks.text: From Eq. 10.1, B = F/IL: the magnetic field strength is numerically equal to the force exerted on a conductor of length one metre carrying a current of one ampere placed perpendicular to the magnetic field. The SI unit of B is the tesla (T): 1 T = 1 N A^-1 m^-1. Magnetic induction is a vector quantity whose direction is that of the magnetic field.

We can also consider a vector L whose magnitude equals the length of the conductor and whose direction is along the flow of current. If the conductor makes an angle theta with the magnetic field, we use the component of L perpendicular to B, that is L sin theta (Fig. 10.4). Then Eq. 10.1 becomes F = BIL sin theta ... (10.2). In vector form, F = I L x B ... (10.3). Equation 10.2 shows that the force is maximum (BIL) when the conductor is perpendicular to the field (theta = 90 degrees) and zero when the conductor lies along the field (theta = 0).

The Earth's magnetic field is approximately that of a dipole, like that of a fictitious bar magnet whose south magnetic pole is towards the geographic north pole and whose north magnetic pole is towards the geographic south pole (Interesting Information).

blocks.alt: Top left: a wire carrying current out of the page between N and S poles, the field weaker on one side and stronger on the other, and the force towards the weaker side. Top middle: Fleming's left-hand rule as three perpendicular arrows for force, field and current. Top right: flux through an area facing the field, one at 60 degrees and one along it. Bottom: a coil of N turns with field lines through it, and the step from a current to a single moving charge.
blocks.caption: Force on a current in a magnetic field, magnetic flux and flux linkage (original diagram after Figures 10.2 to 10.9 and topics 10.1 to 10.4).
blocks.long_description: A wire carrying a current has its own circular magnetic field; on one side this cancels the field of the magnet and on the other it adds to it, so the wire is pushed towards the weaker side, at right angles to both the current and the field. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction: first finger along the field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force. The force equals B I L sin theta. The flux through an area is B A cos theta, theta being the angle between the field and the normal to the area: largest when the area faces the field and zero when it lies along it. A coil of N turns has a flux linkage N times the flux through one turn. A current is moving charge, so a single charge moving across a field feels q v B sin theta.

blocks.title: Example 10.1
blocks.text: A 20.0 cm wire carrying a current of 10.0 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.30 T. If the wire makes an angle of 40 degrees with the direction of the magnetic field, find the magnitude of the force acting on the wire. Solution: L = 20.0 cm = 0.20 m, I = 10.0 A, B = 0.30 T, theta = 40 degrees. Substituting in Eq. 10.2: F = 10.0 A x 0.30 T x 0.20 m x sin 40 degrees = 0.39 N.

blocks.prompt: A current-carrying conductor PQ of length 2 m is placed perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.5 T and the force on it is 1 N; find the current (numerical 10.12, printed 7.12). Find an expression for the force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform field (comprehensive question 10.2).
blocks.explanation: I = F/(BL) = 1/(0.5 x 2) = 1 A; its direction follows from Fleming's left-hand rule for the force into the page (the book gives Q to P). The force is proportional to I, L and B, F = kBIL with k = 1 in SI, so F = BIL; at an angle theta only L sin theta is across the field, giving F = BIL sin theta, or F = I L x B.

items: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force because its own field adds to the external field on one side and cancels it on the other; the force is towards the weaker side, perpendicular to the current and the field. Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb force.
F = BIL (10.1); B = F/IL in tesla, 1 T = 1 N A^-1 m^-1; F = BIL sin theta (10.2); F = I L x B (10.3); maximum across the field, zero along it. Example 10.1: 0.39 N.
